**Mode 3** always splits the system into **three parts**, with the middle moving one way and the sides moving the other way.

teaching.text: If you keep adding masses and springs, you get a **string**. **Every tiny piece of a string has weight, which is its mass. Every tiny piece also pulls back when it is stretched or compressed, which is its springiness.**
children: In musical instruments, we hear these frequencies as **notes**. The ear can pick out many instruments at once because the ear itself is built from masses and springs.
Higher modes have more parts moving against each other. So the springs stretch and compress much more, and those modes vibrate faster.
The string has the same mode patterns. Everything moves together in Mode 1, the two halves move against each other in Mode 2, and the middle moves against the sides in Mode 3.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: Take a string fixed at both ends whose first mode vibrates at **100 hertz**. Its next modes vibrate at **200, 300, 400 and 500 hertz**, so every mode is an **exact multiple** of the first. These multiples are called **harmonics**.
children: The second mode holds **two** copies of the first mode's bump, the third holds **three**, and the fifth holds **five**. So each mode's frequency is the first frequency times the number of copies.

teaching.text: A single mode by itself makes a **pure tone**, which sounds so annoying that it is used for sirens. The sounds we normally hear have many modes at the same time. That is why a real string's motion looks messy and irregular, much like the waveform of speech.

The **spectrum** shows this mixture. **Frequency** goes along the horizontal axis, and **amplitude**, which is strength, goes up the vertical axis. For this string, the spectrum has spikes at 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 hertz.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: All of the results so far come from a short list of **principles of mass-spring systems**, and they all fit together.
children: **More mass lowers the frequency, and more stiffness raises the frequency.**
**A system with n masses has n modes of vibration**, and each higher mode has a higher frequency.
**Adding mass at a spot lowers the frequency more when that spot moves more.** How much a spot moves depends on where it is.
**Where there is the most movement, there is no stretching. Where there is the most stretching, there is no movement.**
**Adding stiffness at a spot raises the frequency more when that spot stretches and compresses more.** This also depends on where the spot is.

In a **fixed-fixed system**, which is fixed at both ends, the harmonics are **whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency**, because each mode holds a whole number of copies of the lowest mode. In a **fixed-free system**, which is fixed at one end and free at the other, they are **odd multiples**, because each mode holds an odd number of copies.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: If you make one piece of a string **heavier**, such as thickening its very middle, some modes change and others do not.
children: In **Mode 1**, the middle moves up and down a lot, so the extra mass **lowers** the frequency.
In **Mode 2**, the middle does not move at all, so the extra mass changes **nothing**.
In **Mode 3**, the middle moves again, so the frequency drops. In **Mode 4**, the middle is still again, so nothing changes. As you go up through the modes, the effect **switches back and forth**.

teaching.text: **Along a vibrating string, places of motion and places of stretching take turns.** Where a piece moves the most, it is just carried up and down and is hardly stretched. Where the string is stretched the most, such as right next to a fixed end, there is **no movement** at all.
children: **The shortcut is that the springiest spots are the spots that do not move.** In **Mode 5** of a string fixed at both ends, the string does not move at the **two fixed ends** or at the **four points where it crosses its middle line**. So those **six places** are the springiest.
The **most motion**, and so the **least springiness**, is at the tops of the **five bumps**.

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently

teaching.text: Changing one small piece of a string can push two modes in **opposite directions**. Take a spot where **Mode 4 moves the most** and where **Mode 5 crosses its middle line**, so Mode 5 does not move there at all. Now add both **mass** and **stiffness** to that piece.
children: **For Mode 4**, the piece is moving, so the extra mass **lowers** the frequency. The piece is barely stretched, so the extra stiffness does nothing.
**For Mode 5**, the piece does not move, so the extra mass does nothing. The piece is stretched the most, so the extra stiffness **raises** the frequency.
So the same change **lowers Mode 4's frequency and raises Mode 5's frequency**. Work out each mode separately by asking whether the spot is moving or stretching in that mode.

teaching.text: **Perturbation theory** predicts how a small change in one location affects how something vibrates. In the late nineteenth century, researchers tested this by placing small amounts of **wax** on different parts of a **drum**.
children: When wax was placed where the drum vibrated a lot, the extra mass made the drum vibrate more slowly, causing its frequency (pitch) to **decrease**.
When wax was placed where the drum did not vibrate, it had **no effect** on the drum's frequency or sound.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: The **larynx** holds the **vocal folds**. The vocal folds form a **membrane**, which is a bit like a drum, so they have many modes of vibration. In Mode 1, all the masses move up and down together. In Mode 2, the two halves move against each other. Higher modes divide the surface into more and more parts.
children: The vocal folds are fixed around their edges, so they behave like a system fixed at both ends. That means their frequencies are harmonics, which are whole-number multiples of the lowest one.

teaching.text: Changing the mass and stiffness of the vocal folds changes the voice. People who smoke heavily can develop **nodules**, which are small growths on the vocal folds. A nodule adds mass at one spot and changes the stiffness of the parts near it. So the folds vibrate differently, and the voice sounds different.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: The **theory** is that the vocal folds vibrate in many modes at once, so a measured voice should have a spectrum with **equidistant harmonics**, which means harmonics that are evenly spaced. A voice was recorded and examined in **Praat**. Its lowest harmonic was about 130 hertz, and the next harmonics were close to two and three times that value. So **the measurement matched the prediction.**
children: This is how the **scientific method** works. Scientists write a clear theory as **differential equations**, solve them to get a prediction, and then measure to check it.
Each person's lowest frequency is different, but the harmonics above it are always close to multiples of it.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **building** is **fixed at one end and free at the other**. The bottom is fixed to the ground, while the top can sway in very strong winds or an earthquake. Engineers design a building to sway only in **Mode 1**. That can feel unpleasant on a high floor, but it is safe. Swaying in a higher mode could break the building.

The **air inside the vocal tract** is also a fixed-free system. At the bottom, the **vocal folds are closed**, so the air there **cannot move**, and that end is **fixed**. At the lips, the air can move in and out easily, so that end is **free**.
children: Unlike a building, the air in the vocal tract vibrates in **all of its modes**. When we speak, we change the mass and stiffness of the air in different places.

teaching.text: A fixed-free system has **frequencies at 100, 300, 500 and 700 hertz**, which are only the odd multiples of 100. The first mode goes from **no motion** at the fixed end to **lots of motion** at the free end, which is only a quarter of a wave. The next possible modes hold **three** and then **five** of these quarter-wave pieces.
children: Two pieces would end with no motion at both ends, which is the pattern of a system fixed at both ends. So even multiples never occur.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract can be modeled as a **chain of masses and springs**. The chain is fixed at the glottis end and free at the lip end. The masses stand for the air's tendency to keep moving, and the springs stand for the air's springiness.
children: The lowest mode corresponds to the **first formant**, **F1**, and the next mode corresponds to the **second formant**, **F2**. The frequencies of a fixed-free system are called **formants**, while the frequencies of a fixed-fixed system are called harmonics.
The second mode vibrates **three times faster** than the first, because it holds three of the first mode's quarter-wave pieces.

teaching.text: Three places along the tube matter for vowels. For **/a/**, the air is squeezed **one third of the way from the glottis**. For **/i/**, it is squeezed **two thirds of the way from the glottis**. For **/u/**, it is squeezed at the **free end, at the lips**.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: A **constriction** is a place where the tongue or lips narrow the vocal tract and squeeze the air. The **glottis** is the tiny space between the vocal folds at the fixed end, so distances are measured from there.
children: In **done**, the central vowel, there is **no constriction**.
In **dean**, a **high front** vowel, the air is squeezed under the roof of the mouth, about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
In **Don**, a **low back** vowel, the air is squeezed far back in the throat, about **one third of the way from the glottis**.
In **dune**, a **high back** vowel made with **lip rounding**, the air is squeezed **at the lips**. **Dan** is a **low front** vowel.

sections.title: Blank source page
Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: **Squeezing air raises both its stiffness and its mass.** Squeezed air is like the air in a tire, which gets **stiffer** when it is squeezed. Packing air into a smaller space also raises its **density**, which makes it more **massive**.

You might think that raising mass and stiffness together would **cancel out**. **That is false** for any system with many masses and springs, because in a given mode each spot is either mostly **moving** or mostly **stretching**.
children: At a spot with no motion and lots of stretching, only the extra stiffness counts, so the frequency **rises**.
At a spot with lots of motion and no stretching, only the extra mass counts, so the frequency **falls**.
Speech itself proves the effects do not cancel, because constrictions in different places clearly change the frequencies of the voice.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: For **/u/**, rounding the lips squeezes the air at the **free end**. This raises the mass and the stiffness of the air there.
children: In **Mode 1**, the air at the free end moves a lot and is hardly compressed. So **motion matters most**, and the extra mass lowers **F1**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at the free end also moves a lot. So **motion matters most** again, and the extra mass lowers **F2**.
So for /u/, **both F1 and F2 go down**.

teaching.text: A speaker started from the central vowel, with formants near 500, 1500 and 2500 hertz, and moved into /u/. **Both formants dropped**, just as predicted.
children: The rounded lips added mass to the air right where it moves the most. The extra stiffness did nothing there, because the air at the lips is moving, not stretching.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the air is squeezed about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**. That one location acts differently in the two modes.
children: In **Mode 1**, the air at this spot moves a lot and is hardly compressed. So **motion matters most**, and the extra mass **lowers F1**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at this spot is compressed a lot. So **springiness matters most**, and the extra stiffness **raises F2**.
In plain terms, the same squeeze lands on a moving spot for F1 and on a springy spot for F2. So one formant falls while the other rises.

teaching.text: A speaker went from the central vowel into /i/. The **first formant dropped a lot**, and the **second formant went up**.
children: The two formants move apart because the same squeeze is at a moving spot for one mode and at a springy spot for the other.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the air is squeezed about **one third of the way from the glottis**, and the pattern is reversed.
children: In **Mode 1**, this spot is near the fixed end, and the air there is compressed a lot. So **springiness matters most**, and the extra stiffness **raises F1**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at this spot moves a lot. So **motion matters most**, and the extra mass **lowers F2**.
So for /a/, **F1 goes up and F2 goes down**, and the two formants get closer together.

teaching.text: You can also reason backward. **If a squeeze raises a formant a lot, the air at that spot must be springy and hardly moving in that mode.** **If a squeeze lowers a formant a lot, the air at that spot must be moving a lot.**

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: The same principles explain all the vowels. **Extra mass matters where the air moves, and extra stiffness matters where the air compresses and expands.** The vocal tract is fixed at the glottis and free at the lips, so its formants are **odd multiples** of the lowest one.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: The air in the tube can be modeled as **lines of air particles**. Each particle stands for billions of real air molecules. The closed vocal folds are at the **fixed end**, and the open lips are at the **free end**.
children: Where the lines bunch close together and then spread far apart, the air is **compressing and expanding**, which is **springiness**.
Where the lines just move back and forth without changing their spacing, the air is acting as a **mass**. This is easiest to see at the **free end**.

teaching.text: **F1** has one point of no motion, at the fixed end. **F2** has two, and **F3** has three. For the **schwa**, which has no constriction, a measured voice had formants near **500, 1500 and 2500 hertz**. These are the odd multiples that the theory predicts.
children: Between each pair of no-motion points, places of most motion and places of most compression take turns, just like on a vibrating string.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: A short question like **Where were you a year ago?** uses all of the constriction rules at once. Each sound squeezes the air in a different place, so the formants keep moving up and down instead of staying at fixed values.
children: When the tongue makes an **/i/**-like squeeze near the front of the mouth, **F1 goes down and F2 goes up**. This happens because that spot is moving in Mode 1 and springy in Mode 2.
When the lips round for **you**, **F1 and F2 both go down**. This happens because the air at the lips is moving in every mode.
When the tongue moves back and down, as in an **/a/**-like sound, **F1 rises and F2 falls**. This happens because that spot is springy in Mode 1 and moving in Mode 2.

teaching.text: **Speech is a continuous series of squeezes, not a list of separate vowels.** So the frequencies of the air in the vocal tract are always changing. The same mass and spring principles predict which way each formant moves at every moment.

lecture13.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production · Source and Filter

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: Every vibrating system in speech follows a small set of principles, and they all fit together.
children: **More mass lowers the frequency, and more stiffness raises the frequency.**
**A system with n masses has n modes**, and each higher mode has a higher frequency. This happens because more parts move against each other, so more springs stretch and compress.

**Adding mass at a spot lowers the frequency more when that spot moves more.** **Adding stiffness at a spot raises the frequency more when that spot stretches and compresses more.** Both depend on where the change is made.
**Where there is the most movement, there is no stretching. Where there is the most stretching, there is no movement.**

In a **fixed-fixed system**, which is fixed at both ends, the frequencies are called **harmonics**. They are **whole-number multiples** of the lowest frequency. In a **fixed-free system**, which is fixed at one end and free at the other, the frequencies are called **formants**, and they are **odd multiples**.

teaching.text: If you raise both the mass and the stiffness of a system, you might think the two effects **cancel out**. That is only true for a **single mass on a single spring**. In a system with many masses and springs, a spot that moves a lot is hardly stretching, and a spot that stretches a lot is hardly moving. So at any one spot, only one of the two changes matters.
children: Picture a spot on a string that never moves but is stretched hard. Extra mass there does nothing, but extra stiffness makes the string pull back harder. So the frequency goes up.
Picture a spot that swings up and down the most. Extra stiffness there does nothing, but extra mass makes that spot harder to move. So the frequency goes down.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: Adding masses adds modes, and the same shapes keep repeating. In **Mode 1**, everything moves together. In **Mode 2**, the system splits into two halves that move against each other. In **Mode 3**, the middle moves against the sides.
children: The more the parts move against each other, the more the springs work. So **higher modes are stiffer and vibrate faster**. In plain terms, a higher mode does not use stiffer springs. It makes the same springs do more stretching.

sections.title: Why fixed–fixed frequencies are integer multiples

teaching.text: In a string fixed at both ends, the first mode is **one half-wave**. This is a single bump that goes from no motion at one end, to the most motion in the middle, to no motion at the other end. Each higher mode fits **more of these half-wave pieces** into the same length.
children: **Mode 2 holds two pieces**, with one half moving up while the other half moves down. Each piece acts like a copy of Mode 1, so Mode 2 has **twice the stiffness** and **twice the frequency**.
**Mode 3 holds three pieces**, and **Mode 5 holds five**. So the fifth mode has five times the frequency of the first.
The short exam answer is that **the fifth mode fits five copies of the first mode**, so it has five times the stiffness and five times the frequency.

teaching.text: The numbers do not have to start at 100. If a voice's lowest frequency is **250 hertz**, its next harmonics are at 500, 750 and 1000 hertz, because each one is still a whole number of copies of the first.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in all of these modes at once. Its **spectrum** has **evenly spaced spikes**, one for each harmonic. **Frequency** goes along the bottom, and **amplitude**, which is strength, goes up. If the first harmonic is 100 hertz, the next ones are 200, 300, 400 and 500 hertz.
children: The **vocal folds** are fixed on all sides, just behind the Adam's apple. So they behave like this kind of fixed-fixed system and produce harmonics.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: The vocal folds form a **membrane**, and the same counting of pieces works on a surface. The first mode is a single bump across the whole membrane. The second mode fits two of those bumps, so it has twice the frequency. The fourth mode fits four ups and downs, so it has four times the frequency.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **building** is **fixed at the bottom** and **free at the top**. In strong winds or an earthquake, engineers want it to sway only in **Mode 1**, with every floor moving together. That can feel a little unpleasant on a high floor, but it is safe. In a higher mode, some floors would move one way while other floors moved the other way, and the whole building could break apart.

A string can be set up the same way, fixed at the bottom and free at the top. Its first mode is no longer a full half-wave. It goes from **no motion at the fixed end** to **lots of motion at the free end**, which is only **one quarter of a wave**.

sections.title: Why fixed–free frequencies are odd multiples

teaching.text: In a fixed-free system, each mode is built from **quarter-wave packets**, which are pieces that are each a quarter of a wave long. Each piece runs from no motion to lots of motion. **Mode 1 holds one piece, Mode 2 holds three, Mode 3 holds five and Mode 4 holds seven.** So if the lowest mode is 100 hertz, the modes are at 100, 300, 500 and 700 hertz.

**Two pieces can never fit.** Two quarter-wave pieces would go from no motion, to lots of motion, to no motion again. That would put a still point at the top as well as the bottom, which would make the system **fixed at both ends**. Adding one more piece, for **three** in total, ends with lots of motion at the top again, so three is the next possible mode.
children: The simple version is that the free end must always be moving, and only an odd number of quarter-wave pieces ends with motion at the free end.

teaching.text: The frequencies of a fixed-free system are called **formants**. **A formant is a frequency at which a system vibrates when it is fixed at one end and completely free at the other.** Formants are **odd multiples** of the lowest one, and they are written **F1**, **F2** and **F3**.

sections.title: Count quarter-waves from the boundary conditions

teaching.text: If you count quarter-wave pieces, you can get every formant from the first one. If **F1 is 500 hertz**, then **F2 is three times that, 1500 hertz**, and **F3 is five times that, 2500 hertz**.
children: Each step from one formant to the next is twice the first formant, because each new mode adds two more quarter-wave pieces.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air inside the mouth and throat forms a tube. At one end are the **vocal folds**. They are closed, so the air there **cannot move back and forth**, and that end is **fixed**. At the other end the **lips are open**, so the air can move back and forth freely, and that end is **free**.
children: So **the air in the vocal tract moves the same way a building sways**. The math for both is almost exactly the same, and the frequencies of both are **formants**.
When we speak, we change the stiffness and mass of the air in different parts of the tract. That moves the formants, and that is how listeners hear different vowels and consonants.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: The air in the tube can be modeled as lines of particles, where each particle stands for billions of air molecules.
children: Where the lines come **very close together and then spread far apart**, the air is compressing and stretching, so it is acting like a **spring**.
Where the lines just **move back and forth** without changing their spacing, the air is acting like a **mass**. This is easiest to see at the **free end, at the lips**.
An easy way to read the model is that bunching and spreading means springiness, and sliding without bunching means mass.

teaching.text: The air's modes match a building's modes. In **Mode 1**, the only point of no motion is the fixed end. **Mode 2** has **two** points of no motion, and **Mode 3** has **three**. Around each of these points, the air compresses and expands a lot.

In **Mode 4** of a building, **the springiest places are the fixed bottom and the three points where the building crosses its resting position**, which makes four places in all. These are the springiest places because they do not move.
children: If you add stiffness where the building moves the most, **nothing changes**, because the building is not acting like a spring there. If you add stiffness where the building does not move, the frequency **goes way up**.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: A **constriction** is a place where the tongue or lips squeeze the air. Its location is measured from the **glottis**, which is the tiny space between the vocal folds at the fixed end.
children: In **done**, the central vowel, there is **no constriction**.
In **dean**, a **front high vowel**, the air is squeezed under the roof of the mouth, about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
In **Don**, a **low back vowel**, the air is squeezed far back, about **one third of the way from the glottis**.
In **dune**, a **back high vowel**, the lips are rounded close together, which squeezes the air **at the lips**. **Dan** is a **front low vowel**.

sections.title: Why a constriction can raise one formant and lower another

teaching.text: **Compressing air raises its stiffness**, just as squeezing a tire makes it stiffer. So a constriction where the air is compressed a lot **raises the frequency**. **Packing air together raises its mass**, because it raises the air's **density**. So a constriction where the air moves a lot **lowers the frequency**.

So every constriction **adds both mass and stiffness**, but that does not mean the effects cancel out. **Along a vibrating string or a vibrating column of air, the spots that move the most take turns with the spots that compress and expand the most.**
children: To answer any constriction question, ask two things in order. First, is the air at this spot mostly moving or mostly compressing in this mode? Second, does the extra mass or the extra stiffness count there?

teaching.text: The same two steps answer a question about a string fixed at both ends. Take a small spot where **Mode 3 crosses its middle line** and **Mode 4 is at the top of a bump**. Now add both mass and stiffness to that spot.
children: In **Mode 3**, the string does not move at that spot but is stretched the most. So only the extra stiffness counts, and **Mode 3's frequency goes up**.
In **Mode 4**, the string moves the most at that spot and hardly stretches. So only the extra mass counts, and **Mode 4's frequency goes down**.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: Before reasoning about any vowel, it helps to know where the air moves and where it compresses in the first two modes.
children: In **Mode 1**, the air near the closed glottis end compresses and expands a lot. The air near the open lip end just moves back and forth.
In **Mode 2**, the air compresses a lot at the closed end and again about two thirds of the way along. In between, about one third of the way along, the air mostly moves.

**In every mode, the air at the closed end is always springy, and the air at the open end is always moving.** Air can be squeezed against a closed end, but at an open end there is nothing to squeeze it against.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The mass-spring chain marks the three vowel locations along the tube. **/a/** is **one third of the way from the glottis**, **/i/** is **two thirds of the way**, and **/u/** is at the **lip end**. Each vowel adds mass and stiffness at its own spot. Its effect on F1 and F2 depends on whether the air there is moving or compressing in each mode.

If you add mass and stiffness at the **very top of a building**, the frequency of **every mode goes down**, including Mode 4. The top is the free end, so in every mode it moves the most and is almost never stretched. So only the extra mass counts there.
children: **The top of the building corresponds to the lip end of the vocal tract.** That is why rounding the lips lowers every formant.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: **/u/** rounds the lips, which squeezes the air at the **free end**. In both Mode 1 and Mode 2, the air at the free end moves a lot and is hardly compressed. So the extra **mass** counts in both modes, and **F1 and F2 both go down**.
children: A speaker moved from the central vowel into /u/, and the recording showed **both formants dropping**, just as predicted.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: **/i/** squeezes the air about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
children: In **Mode 1**, the air at that spot moves a lot, so the extra mass counts and **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at that spot is compressed a lot, so the extra stiffness counts and **F2 goes up**.
A speaker moved from the central vowel into /i/. The **first formant dropped a lot**, and the **second formant went up**.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: **/a/** squeezes the air about **one third of the way from the glottis**, which reverses the /i/ pattern.
children: In **Mode 1**, that spot is near the fixed end, and the air there is compressed a lot. So the extra stiffness counts and **F1 goes up**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at that spot moves a lot. So the extra mass counts and **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: You can also reason backward. **If a squeeze raises a formant a lot, the air at that spot must be very springy and hardly moving in that mode.** **If a squeeze lowers a formant a lot, the air at that spot must be moving a lot.**

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: A **schwa** has no constriction. A measured schwa had formants near **500, 1500 and 2500 hertz**, which are the odd multiples that a plain fixed-free tube predicts. Every other vowel moves the formants away from these schwa values, by changing where the air moves and where it compresses.

sections.title: The source supplies harmonics and the filter shapes their heights

teaching.text: Speech uses **two vibrating systems at the same time**.
children: The **vocal folds** are a fixed-fixed system. They are the **source**, and they produce **harmonics**. The lowest harmonic is called the **base frequency**, or **F0**. In this example, the harmonics are **100 hertz apart**.
The **air in the vocal tract** is a fixed-free system. It acts as a **filter**, and its frequencies are the **formants**. For the schwa, the formants are near **500, 1500, 2500 and 3500 hertz**.

teaching.text: **The formants control how tall the harmonics are.** All the harmonics are still there. But **harmonics near a formant are tall, and harmonics far from any formant are short**. The outline of their heights is called the **envelope**, and it rises into a peak at each formant.
children: **The harmonics stay the same from vowel to vowel. Only their heights change, and the envelope is what makes each vowel sound different.**
In plain terms, the vocal folds decide which frequencies are present, and the shape of the mouth decides which of those frequencies are loud.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the filter keeps **F1 low and F2 high**. The tall harmonics are bunched at the very bottom of the spectrum. Then comes a long stretch of short harmonics, and the next tall group is much higher up. So the two lowest formants are **far apart**.
children: The squeeze two thirds of the way from the glottis puts the formants there, because it lowers F1 and raises F2.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the filter **raises F1 and lowers F2**. So the first two groups of tall harmonics are **close together** in the lower part of the spectrum.
children: The same harmonics from the vocal folds are under both /i/ and /a/. Only the filter is different. Moving the squeeze moves the formants, and that changes which harmonics are loud.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time

teaching.text: **A spectrum shows one instant**, but speech is **time-varying**, which means it changes over time, because the vocal tract keeps moving and squeezes keep forming and opening up. **A spectrogram lines up many spectra side by side over time.**
children: **Time** goes along the **horizontal axis**.
**Frequency**, which was on the horizontal axis of each spectrum, moves to the **vertical axis**.
**Amplitude**, which was the height of each spike, becomes **darkness**. The louder a frequency is, the darker it looks.

teaching.text: The formants show up as **dark bands** that move as the speaker moves. In **/ia/**, the two lowest bands start **far apart** during /i/. As the speaker moves into /a/, **F1 rises and F2 falls**, so the bands **come close together**.
children: Reading a spectrogram means following the dark bands, because those bands are the formants changing over time.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: **Where were you a year ago?** is a good sentence for seeing the source and the filter working together over time. The vocal folds, which are the source, keep producing harmonics. Meanwhile the vocal tract, which is the filter, keeps changing shape. So the envelope over the harmonics changes from moment to moment.
children: On a spectrogram, these changes show up as **dark bands that rise and fall**, because the dark bands are the formants and darkness shows amplitude.
Where the vowel sounds like **/i/**, the two lowest bands spread far apart. During **you**, all the bands drop, because the lips are rounded.

teaching.text: **A spectrum shows one frozen instant, but a spectrogram shows how the formants move**, and real speech is always moving. To read a sentence like this one, follow each band and ask which squeeze moved it.

sections.title: Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify

teaching.text: Formants can only show up through the harmonics, so the spacing of the harmonics matters. Suppose the harmonics are every **100 hertz** and the formants are at **300 and 2100 hertz**. Then **many harmonics** sit under each formant peak, so the formants are easy to see.

With a higher base frequency, such as **250 hertz**, fewer harmonics land on each formant peak. A formant can even fall **between two harmonics**. Then **it becomes very hard to tell the harmonics apart from the formants**.
children: A **toddler's** harmonics can be at 400, 800 and 1200 hertz, and a **soprano's** can start at 800 hertz. That is why their vowels can be very hard to identify.

teaching.text: **The formants make a smooth outline, and the harmonics are single points along that outline.** A higher F0 means fewer points, so the spectrogram stops looking like clean formant bands.
children: A simple way to see it is that the harmonics are like dots used to trace a curve. With many dots, the curve is obvious. With only a few dots, the curve is hard to see.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion

teaching.text: Speech uses **two main vibrating systems**. The first is the **vocal folds**. They form a **membrane** that is **fixed on all sides** and made of many masses and springs. The vocal folds vibrate in many modes at once. In Mode 1, all the masses move up and down together. In Mode 2, half move up while the other half move down. Higher modes have more complicated patterns. All five modes add together into one combined motion.
children: The vocal folds are a fixed-fixed system, so their frequencies are **harmonics**. Harmonics are whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency.
The **lowest harmonic** is called **F0**. Each person has a different F0, but the other harmonics are always multiples of it.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics

teaching.text: The second system is the **air in the vocal tract**. It is **fixed at the glottis**, because the closed vocal folds stop the air there from moving back and forth. It is **free at the lips**, where the air can move in and out. Because one end is fixed and the other is free, only the **odd multiples** occur. So its frequencies are one, three, five and seven times the lowest one.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes

teaching.text: Each fixed-free mode is built from **quarter-wavelength packets**, which are pieces that are each a quarter of a wave long. Each piece runs from no motion at a still point to the most motion at a moving point. **Mode 1 holds one piece, Mode 2 holds three, Mode 3 holds five and Mode 4 holds seven.**
children: Two pieces would end with a still point at the free end, which cannot happen. So only odd numbers of pieces fit, and that is why the formants are odd multiples of the first.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: In the vocal tract, the air moves **longitudinally**, which means back and forth along the tube, not up and down. Each formant is one mode of this back-and-forth motion. F1 is the lowest mode, and F2 is the next one.
children: These modes look like a building's modes turned on their side. The fixed glottis end is on the left, and the free lip end is on the right.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression

teaching.text: **In every mode, the air at the closed end is always springy, and the air at the open end is always moving.** Air can be squeezed against a closed end, but at an open end there is nothing to squeeze it against.
children: Near the **closed end**, the thin slices of air come very close together and then spread far apart. So the air **compresses and expands**, and it acts like a **spring**.
Near the **open end**, the slices stay the same distance apart and simply move back and forth. So the air acts like a **mass**.
In plain terms, the lip end swings like a heavy door, and the throat end squeezes like a pillow.

teaching.text: In higher modes, springy places and moving places **take turns** more and more times along the tube.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode

teaching.text: You can work out what a constriction does at any spot, in any mode, using the same steps. Take a spot inside the tube where, in **Mode 3**, the lines of air bunch up and spread apart but hardly move back and forth. Squeezing the tract at that spot raises **F3**.
children: Step one is that squeezing air always **adds both mass and stiffness**, just as squeezing a tire makes it stiffer.
Step two is that at this spot in Mode 3, the air is acting like a **pure spring**. It compresses and expands but does not move back and forth, so the extra mass does not matter.
Step three is that only the extra stiffness counts, and **more stiffness raises the frequency**, so **F3 goes up**.

teaching.text: Do not memorize the answer. **Build it one step at a time**, with each step based on the one before it. That is how any good argument is built, in science or in art.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed

teaching.text: Images taken while people speak show where each vowel squeezes the air. The tube runs from the closed glottis to the open lips.
children: The vowel in **done** has **no constriction** at all.
**dean** squeezes the air near the front, about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
**Don** squeezes the air far back in the throat, about **one third of the way from the glottis**.
**dune** squeezes the air **at the lips** by rounding them. **Dan** is a low front vowel.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness

teaching.text: A constriction changes two things about the air. It changes the air's **mass**, which is how hard the air is to start or stop moving. It also changes the air's **stiffness**, which is how hard the air pushes back when it is squeezed. In the mass-spring model, a constriction is drawn as **heavier masses and stiffer springs** at that spot.
children: A constriction always raises both. But moving places and springy places take turns along the tube, so **its effect depends on what the air is doing at that spot in each mode**.
**When stiffness is what matters at a spot, the frequency goes up. When mass is what matters, the frequency goes down.**

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location

teaching.text: The same location in the tube can act differently in the two modes, so you have to check each mode separately. A spot can be moving in Mode 1 and springy in Mode 2. Then one squeeze lowers F1 and raises F2 at the same time.
children: That is why a vowel is defined by its pair of formants, not by one formant alone.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model

teaching.text: **/u/** squeezes the air at the lips. At the open end, the air moves back and forth and is hardly compressed in **every** mode, so the air there acts like a pure mass. So the extra stiffness does not matter, but the extra mass does, and **F1 and F2 both go down**.
children: Schwa's formants are about **500 and 1500 hertz**. A measured /u/ had an F1 in the low two hundreds, well below 500.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: **/i/** squeezes the air about two thirds of the way from the glottis.
children: In **Mode 1**, the air at that spot moves back and forth, so it acts like a mass. The extra mass counts, and **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at that spot compresses and expands, so it acts like a spring. The extra stiffness counts, and **F2 goes up**.
A speaker moving from schwa into /i/ showed exactly this, with **F1 going down and F2 going up**.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern

teaching.text: **/a/** squeezes the air about one third of the way from the glottis.
children: In **Mode 1**, that spot is close to the closed end, so the air there is mostly springy. The extra stiffness counts, and **F1 goes up**.
In **Mode 2**, that spot sits between two springy regions, so the air there is mostly moving. The extra mass counts, and **F2 goes down**.
A speaker saying /a/ showed **F1 going up and F2 going down**. In a typical /a/, F1 and F2 are fairly close together.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: The logic is the same for all three vowels. **First, find out whether the air at the squeeze is mostly moving or mostly compressing in each mode. Then decide whether the extra mass or the extra stiffness counts.**
children: At the lips, the air is moving in both modes, so /u/ lowers both formants.
Two thirds of the way along, the air is moving in Mode 1 and springy in Mode 2, so /i/ lowers F1 and raises F2.
One third of the way along, the air is springy in Mode 1 and moving in Mode 2, so /a/ raises F1 and lowers F2.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing

teaching.text: The vocal folds are the **source**. Their mass and stiffness set **F0**, and F0 sets the spacing of the harmonics.
children: **Big, heavy, loose vocal folds** have a lot of mass and little stiffness, so their **F0 is low**, around 100 hertz, with harmonics at 200, 300 and so on.
**Tighter, lighter vocal folds** have a higher F0, such as 250 hertz. **Very tight, light vocal folds** have an even higher F0, such as 350 hertz.

teaching.text: **F0 does not stay the same while people talk.** Speakers keep changing F0 by tightening and loosening their vocal folds, and listeners use those changes to understand meaning.
children: When **The dog slept here** is said as a statement, F0 falls at the very end. When the same words are said as a question, F0 rises at the end.
The way F0 moves also tells listeners whether a person is being sarcastic, pretending, or even lying.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics

teaching.text: The air in the vocal tract is the **filter**. Its formants depend on **where the squeeze is**. Schwa has F1 near 500 and F2 near 1500. /u/ has lower formants. /i/ has F1 and F2 very far apart, and /a/ has them very close together.
**The core rule is that a formant makes the harmonics closest to it louder, and harmonics far from any formant come out quieter.**
children: **The shape of the vowel is the filter. The vocal folds supply the harmonics, and the filter decides which harmonics come through loudly.**

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches

teaching.text: **The lower F0 is, the more harmonics the formants can shape.** When harmonics are every 100 hertz, many harmonics sit under each formant. So the spectrum clearly shows the formant peaks.

With very light, tight vocal folds, a formant at 500 hertz may have **no harmonic near it to make louder**. With so few harmonics, a formant can fall between them and get missed, or it can be hard to tell where the formant is.
children: An **opera singer** is an extreme example, which is why sung vowels are hard to identify. Singers are even trained to shape the mouth so the formants line up with the harmonics.
A **small child** has an F0 near 500 hertz, so very few harmonics fall near the formants. That is why only the people who take care of the child understand the child's speech easily.
A simple way to see it is that the formants are the same in every case, but a high voice gives the listener only a few harmonics to hear them through.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram

teaching.text: A **spectrogram** lines up many spectra side by side over time. **Time** goes along the horizontal axis, **frequency** goes up the vertical axis, and **darkness** shows how much energy, or amplitude, there is.

You can measure F0 in **Praat**. Take a small piece of speech, look at its spectrum, and pick the lowest harmonic. One measured voice had an F0 of about 170 hertz, and the next harmonic was at about twice that value.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: Saying **Where were you a year ago?** brings every idea about speech together in one short sentence. The vocal folds supply harmonics the whole time. Every new sound changes where the tongue and lips squeeze the air, so the formants keep moving from one moment to the next.
children: On a spectrogram of the sentence, **time** goes along the bottom, **frequency** goes up, and the **dark bands are the formants**.
Where the vowel sounds like **/i/**, **F2 rises high and F1 stays low**. This happens because the squeeze lands where Mode 2 is springy and Mode 1 is moving.
During **you**, the formants **drop**. Rounding the lips adds mass right where the air moves the most, and that lowers all of them.
Through **a year ago**, F2 goes up and then down again as the tongue moves from one vowel to the next.

teaching.text: **The formants are always changing during speech, so speech is not a string of frozen vowels.** You can predict every rise and fall of a formant with the same mass and spring reasoning. Ask where the squeeze is, and whether the air there is moving or compressing in each mode.
children: This constant change is why a network that sees two formants from one frozen moment cannot understand real speech. Speech recognition needs systems that take in whole stretches of sound over time.
In plain terms, a spectrogram of a real sentence is a moving record of the tongue and lips. To read it, you follow the dark bands as they rise and fall.

sections.title: Speech-complexity experiment prompt

teaching.text: A recording that was cut and joined back together shows how complicated speech perception is. The **m** part of a recorded **ma** was joined to the **a** part of a recorded **na**. Listeners clearly heard **na**, not ma.
children: **Whether listeners hear m or n depends more on the vowel than on the nasal sound itself.** After m, one formant of the vowel stays fairly **flat**. After n, that formant shows a **big drop**.

So listeners decide which consonant they heard **during the vowel**, after the consonant is already over. This was one of the first surprising results in speech perception, published in the **1950s** by the linguist **André Malécot**.

teaching.text: Listeners **take in whole stretches of speech and then decide** about the sounds that came first. For about seventy years, speech recognition machines that treated each slice of sound separately **failed**. Modern speech recognition uses large language models, which use what comes later to decide about what came before.

sections.title: Use formants as input to vowel recognition

teaching.text: A **neural network** can be trained to recognize vowels from formants. Its **two inputs** are **F1 and F2**, measured from real recordings of five vowels. Its job is to decide which vowel was spoken.
children: **The network's knowledge is stored in its weights**, and the weights are learned from the data.
Information enters at the input, a little like sound reaching the ear. Each hidden layer turns the numbers it receives into a new set of numbers, a little like the stages of processing in the brain.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network

teaching.text: The network has **five output neurons**, one for each word, **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**. It has **three hidden layers** with **3, 2 and 4 neurons**. Every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next layer, so the network is **fully connected**.
children: This version is **purely linear**, which means it has **no activation functions**. Each neuron just passes on the result of its inner product.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections

teaching.text: Before training, **every weight is a random number between minus one and one**. A **positive** weight makes its input push the next neuron up. A **negative** weight makes its input push the next neuron down.
children: The example input is **F1 of 320 and F2 of 2000 hertz**. That is a very low F1 with a very high F2, which is the pattern of **/i/**, so the correct answer is **dean**.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries the input through the network one layer at a time. Each neuron computes an **inner product**, which means it multiplies each incoming number by its weight and adds the results.
children: For the top neuron of the first hidden layer, F1 is multiplied by its weight, F2 is multiplied by its weight, and the two results are added. That sum is the neuron's activation.
The other neurons do the same with their own weights. So the first hidden layer produces three numbers. These go through the next weights to make two numbers, then four, and then five at the output.
You never need to do these calculations by hand. What matters is that every step is an inner product.

teaching.text: The output is a **probability distribution** over the five words, with values of **.5, .1, .1, .1 and .2**, which add up to one. With random weights, the network gives its highest probability to **done**, so it is wrong.
children: The correct answer is given as the target distribution **0, 0, 1, 0, 0**. **Stochastic gradient descent** then changes each weight, so that next time the inner products give a high probability to dean.
In plain terms, the network starts out guessing. The target tells it what the right guess was, and learning nudges every weight so the right guess wins next time.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch

teaching.text: **PyTorch** describes the network as a list of layers. **Sequential** means the network has **one layer after another, in order**. **Linear** means the layer **does inner products** of the weights and the activations from the layer before.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3)** means **take input from 2 neurons, and have 3 neurons**. The next lines read 3 in and 2 out, then 2 in and 4 out, then 4 in and 5 out.
Setting the **bias** to False keeps every layer purely linear, which matches the diagram of the network.

teaching.text: **Only layers that do calculations get a line of code.** The **input layer** has no weights coming into it and does no inner products. So it never gets its own line, and the first line describes the **first hidden layer**.
children: This network has **five layers in total** but only **three hidden layers**. The **last line is always the output layer**, so read the question carefully.

teaching.text: To **add a hidden layer of 3 neurons right before the output**, change the old last line from 4 in and 5 out to **4 in and 3 out**. Then add a new last line that takes **3 in and gives 5 out**.
children: A quick check is that the first number on each line must match the second number on the line before it.

teaching.text: Suppose a network is written as 4 in and 3 out, 3 in and 8 out, 8 in and 4 out, 4 in and 4 out, and 4 in and 5 out. This network takes **4 numbers as input**, has **four hidden layers** with 3, 8, 4 and 4 neurons, and chooses among **5 categories**.
children: When the first category is correct, the target distribution has a **1 in the first slot and 0 everywhere else**.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: A **neural network** can work as a very simple **speech recognizer**. It takes the **two formants, F1 and F2**, of a vowel and decides which of **five words** it heard, **done, dune, dean, Don or Dan**. Networks like this were used fifteen or twenty years ago. Modern **large language models** are built from many networks like this one, the way molecules are built from **atoms**.

The network has **2 input neurons**, **three hidden layers** with **3, 2 and 4 neurons**, and **5 output neurons**. Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer, so the network is **fully connected**.
children: The **input neurons** just take in numbers from the outside world. For example, one speaker's vowel might have an F1 of 400 and an F2 of 1900.

**The network's knowledge is stored in its weights.** Each connection has a weight, which is a positive or negative number. The whole network is just a machine that processes numbers using those weights.
Each neuron's activation is calculated from the neurons that feed into it. The activations of the last layer become the network's decision.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries one input through the network until it reaches a decision. The example input is **F1 of 320 and F2 of 2000**, which is the pattern of **dean**.
children: Each neuron computes an **inner product**. For the top neuron of the first hidden layer, the weight on F1 is multiplied by 320, the weight on F2 is multiplied by 2000, and the two results are added.
The result of that inner product, before anything else is done to it, is called the neuron's **linear activation**. Here it comes out slightly below zero.
The other neurons do the same thing with their own weights. Their activations then become the inputs to the next layer, which does more inner products. This continues until the output layer.

teaching.text: At the end, the output numbers are turned into a **probability distribution**. This is a set of numbers between zero and one that **add up to one**, and it is the network's **decision**. The step that does this is called **softmax**. All you need to know about softmax is that it turns numbers into probabilities, and a bigger number gets a bigger probability.
children: Probabilities and percentages are the same idea. A probability of 0.55 is a 55 percent chance.
Here the network gives **done about 56 percent** and much less to each of the other words. So it is basically saying **"I heard done,"** even though the input was dean.

teaching.text: **All of the network's knowledge is just positive and negative numbers, and all of its decision making is just multiplying and adding**, which are things learned in second grade. **Inference** means working out a decision. The AI systems people chat with every day make their decisions using only these simple operations.
children: This is less surprising than it sounds, because brains are chemical machines. Inside neurons, the chemistry of ions such as sodium, potassium and calcium does something close to adding and multiplying.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation

teaching.text: Every step is an inner product, so you can figure out the effect of raising one number without doing any math. Take the top neuron of the last hidden layer. Its activation is about 1.57, and its weight into the **done** output is positive 0.1.
children: If that **activation goes up**, its contribution to done goes up, because the contribution is the activation times a positive weight. So the **probability of done goes up**.
If that **weight goes up**, from 0.1 to 0.2, the same contribution gets bigger, because the activation is positive. So the **probability of done goes up** again.
**A positive number times a positive number is positive.** So raising either one makes that neuron push the done output up more.

teaching.text: These questions test whether you understand what happens, not whether you can multiply. A good answer names the direction, up or down, and then gives the reason. For example, "the probability of done goes up because the weight and the activation are both positive, so their product adds more to the done output."
children: In plain terms, each neuron votes for each output through its weight. A positive vote from an active neuron always helps that output.
If the weight were negative instead, raising the activation would push the output down. So the sign of the weight decides the direction.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Every network starts out knowing nothing**, because its weights start out **random**. It only gets better when it is told the right answer.
children: The right answer is given as a **desired output**. For a recording of dean, the desired output is **0, 0, 1, 0, 0**. This says there is a 100 percent chance it was dean and zero chance for every other word. A list like this, with one 1 and zeros everywhere else, is called a **one-hot encoding**.
The output the network actually produces is the **computed output**. The difference between the computed output and the desired output is the network's **error**.
The desired outputs come from real data, such as a table of each student's formants together with the vowel that student actually said.

teaching.text: **Backpropagation** is the method that changes the weights so the network makes better decisions. After learning, if you give the network 320 and 2000 again, the probability of done should go down and the probability of dean should go up.
children: **Learning happens gradually, one small step at a time.** Just like stochastic gradient descent, the weights do not jump to the right values all at once. Each piece of data nudges the weights a little, then the next piece nudges them again, and so on.
Each weight moves a small step in whichever direction makes the error smaller. The **learning rate** sets how big each step is.

The weights are updated **starting from the end**. First the weights into the output change, then the weights into the third hidden layer, then the second, then the first. During this backward pass, the activations from the forward pass stay the same.

teaching.text: This is why AI needs huge **data centers**. A modern chatbot can have **trillions of weights**, and backpropagation has to nudge every one of them, over and over, for months.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: For the **last weight**, it is easy to tell which way to change it. This is the 0.1 that connects the top neuron of the last hidden layer to **done**.
children: That weight multiplies an activation of about 1.57, so raising the weight would raise the probability of done.
The desired probability of done is **zero**, so raising the weight would make the error **worse**.
So that weight should be **lowered**. Lowering it shrinks its contribution and pulls the probability of done down toward zero. Only one inner product is needed to figure this out.

teaching.text: For the **first weight**, it is very hard to tell which way to change it. This is the 0.005 near the input.
children: Changing it changes one activation in the first hidden layer. That changes the second hidden layer, which changes the third, which finally changes the output probabilities.

**Its effect on the decision has to pass through all the layers in between**, and it also depends on all the later weights. So you cannot tell just by looking at it whether it should go up or down. Backpropagation still works it out.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **The last weights directly control the output probabilities.** So they have a direct effect on the error, and the difference between the computed output and the desired output can be used right away to improve them.

**The first weights affect their own activations, and those activations then affect two more layers.** It is very hard to figure out how much an early weight is to blame for a mistake at the very end. Its effect on the error also **includes the effect of the last weights**, because the last weights come after it.

So **improving the last weights is the easy problem**, and improving the first weights is a much bigger problem that already contains the easy one. **Dynamic programming** is a method that solves the small problems first and then uses their answers to solve the bigger problems that depend on them. It was developed by **Bellman** and **Viterbi**.
children: **Backpropagation is stochastic gradient descent plus dynamic programming.** Stochastic gradient descent changes the numbers gradually. Dynamic programming decides the order, which is the **back** in backpropagation.
Backpropagation was worked out in the **mid-1980s**. In 2024, a Nobel Prize recognized it, because there would be no AI without it.

Research from the last ten years suggests that single neurons in the brain also work forward and then backward, using their chemistry. So this forward-then-backward process may not be so different from what brains do.

The short exam answer is this. The last weight affects the decision in one simple step. The first weight's effect passes through many layers and depends on the later weights. So the easy problem is solved first, and its answer is reused for the harder problems.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: Training needs two tables of numbers, which are called **matrices**. Each row pairs **one recording** with **the vowel it really was**.
children: The **input matrix** has one row per recording and **two columns**, F1 and F2, because the network takes in two numbers. With about 110 recordings, it is 110 by 2.
The **output matrix** has one row per recording and **five columns**, one for each word. A **1 marks the true vowel**, and the other columns have 0. It is 110 by 5.
So row by row, the network is told the right answer. For example, formants like 800 and 1700 go with one vowel, and formants like 700 and 1100 go with another.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: A short **Python** program that uses the **PyTorch** library builds and trains this network.
children: The **import** lines tell the program to use the **torch library**. The library does all the background work, so the network can be described in just a few lines.
The two **load** lines read in the two matrices. The formants become X, and the true vowels become Y.

teaching.text: **Sequential** means the network is a **sequence of layers**, one after another. **Linear** means the layer **does inner products**, because a linear layer only multiplies and adds.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3)** describes the **first hidden layer**, which takes **2 inputs and gives 3 outputs**. The next lines take 3 and give 2, take 2 and give 4, and take 4 and give 5.

The network has **five layers**, but there are only **four lines**, because the **input layer does no processing**. It only receives numbers, so the only sign of it in the code is the 2 in the first line.

teaching.text: The last lines run **one training step** using all 110 rows at once. **SGD** is stochastic gradient descent, and **lr** is the **learning rate**, which sets the size of each step.
children: The **loss** measures the network's mistakes by comparing its outputs with the true vowels. **backward** runs backpropagation to work out how each weight should change, and **step** actually changes the weights.
In plain terms, the program describes the network, shows it the data, measures how wrong it is, works backward to find which weights caused the mistake, and then adjusts the weights a little.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: **Lord Edgar Adrian** won the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1932** for discovering that **neurons are nearly digital**. A real neuron is roughly **on or off**. It is either firing or not firing, instead of taking any value at all. The neurons in the network so far are not like that, because their activations can be any number, such as slightly below zero, about 6.6, or about 2.7.
Because of this discovery, people added an **activation function** called the **sigmoid** to neural networks. The sigmoid takes the inner product and squashes it into a number between zero and one.
children: If the inner product is a **large negative number**, the sigmoid gives about **0**, so the neuron is **off**. An inner product of minus 4 gives almost exactly zero, and minus 10, minus 100 and minus 1000 also give about zero.
If the inner product is a **large positive number**, the sigmoid gives about **1**, so the neuron is **on**. An inner product of 4 gives almost exactly one, and 6 or 100 also give about one.

Only inner products **near zero** give values in between. So the sigmoid makes the neuron **nearly digital**, either on or off. This is like the chemistry that keeps real neurons from firing without limit.

teaching.text: The sigmoid also matches something important about **perception** in animals and humans. **Some things that are very different are perceived as the same, and some things that are very similar are perceived as different.**
children: You recognize a friend as the same person whether they wear a hat or not, or a different shirt on a different day. Perception ignores many real differences, just as the sigmoid gives minus 1000, minus 100 and minus 20 all the same value.

USC and UCLA are close to each other, both large, and alike in their labs and their football. Yet people see them as completely different. Small differences can matter a lot, just as two inputs slightly below and slightly above zero land on opposite sides of the sigmoid's jump.
In plain terms, the flat parts of the curve treat very different inputs as the same, and the steep middle separates inputs that are almost the same.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: Adding the sigmoid to each hidden neuron changes every number that comes after it. The inputs are still the formants, but each hidden neuron now passes on its sigmoid value instead of its raw inner product.
children: The first hidden neuron's inner product is slightly below zero, and the sigmoid turns it into about **0.4**.
The second neuron's inner product is about 6.6, and the sigmoid turns it into about **1**, so that neuron is fully on.
Each time a neuron changes, the activations in the later layers are recalculated, and the output probabilities shift.

teaching.text: With the same random weights and the sigmoid on all nine hidden neurons, the decision moves away from done. The network now spreads its probability more evenly and gives its highest probability, about one third, to **Dan**. So it is **still wrong** about dean.
children: The sigmoid changes how the network calculates, but only training with backpropagation can give it good weights.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The program changes in only one way. **nn.Sigmoid** is added after each **hidden** linear layer. It means "apply the sigmoid," and it makes that layer nearly digital.
children: The **last layer has no sigmoid**, because its outputs go straight into the loss calculation, which turns them into probabilities with softmax.
The rest of the training program, with SGD and a learning rate of 0.1, stays the same.

teaching.text: To find out whether the sigmoid makes the vowel recognizer better or worse, you train both versions and compare them. You can also swap in other activation functions that look somewhat like the sigmoid, such as one called **ReLU**, to see whether they improve recognition.
children: **Many of the most basic ideas in AI come from how real brains work.** These include neurons, inner products that collect input from many neurons, and the nearly digital firing that the sigmoid copies.

lecture16.title: Neural Networks · Vowel data, training runs, and initialization

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: This **neural network** copies a very simple piece of human perception. It takes the **two formants**, F1 and F2, of a single vowel said on its own, and it decides which of five words it heard, **done, dune, dean, Don or Dan**. It has 2 input neurons, hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons, and 5 output neurons. Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer.

**The weights are the network's knowledge.** Each weight is a positive or negative number. For each recording, the network is told the right answer as a probability distribution. For a speaker's /i/, it is told **0, 0, 1, 0, 0**, which means a 100 percent chance that the word was dean.
children: At first, **the weights are random**, so the network knows nothing. The distribution it produces is usually very different from the right answer.
That difference is a **mistake**, and the network learns by correcting its mistakes.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries the input through the network. Take **F1 of 320 and F2 of 2000**, which is one speaker's /i/. Each neuron in the first hidden layer computes an **inner product**, which means it multiplies each formant by its weight and adds the results. Those activations go into the next layer, which does its own inner products. This continues until the output gives a probability for each word.
children: With random weights, the network gives its highest probability, more than half, to **done**. So it decides it heard done, even though the right answer is dean.

teaching.text: To fix the mistake, **all the weights have to change**, both the ones near the output and the ones near the input. The method that does this is **backpropagation**, which combines **stochastic gradient descent** and **dynamic programming**.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation

teaching.text: **Changing a weight at the very end changes the output probabilities right away.** The output probabilities are the network's decision, and the last weights are exactly the ones used in the final inner products.
children: For example, the probability of done comes partly from a weight of 0.1 times an activation of about 1.57.

The network said done, but the answer was dean, so the probability of done is **too high**. Raising that 0.1 to 0.5 would make the probability of done even higher, which is the opposite of what we want. So that weight should go **down**.
For the last weights, it is easy to tell whether each one should go up or down.

teaching.text: **Changing a weight near the input sets off a chain of changes.** It changes the activations in the first hidden layer. Those change the second hidden layer, which changes the third, which finally changes the decision.
children: So deciding how to change an early weight is a very hard problem. It is like the dynamic programming puzzle where always picking the smallest next step gives the wrong answer.

sections.title: Vowel formants overlap across five categories

teaching.text: The real formant data from the class shows why AI is hard. Each recording is a dot. **F1 is on the horizontal axis**, and **F2 is on the vertical axis**. There are 525 dots, 105 for each vowel.
children: The data does show a pattern. The **/i/ dots are high up**, with a **high F2 and a low F1**, just as the theory predicts. And /i/ is clearly different from /u/.
But there is **a huge amount of overlap**. Many /æ/ dots sit among the /i/ dots, and many others overlap with schwa. The /u/, /a/ and schwa groups of dots pile on top of each other.
Some dots are probably measurement mistakes. Real data always has errors, the same way speech recorded by a phone on a noisy train has errors. So these dots were left in.

teaching.text: **If each vowel's dots formed its own separate group, AI would be easy.** Because the groups overlap, a network has to see the data many times to learn where each vowel is most likely. Even then, many points are unclear. If a new speaker's formants land in the middle of the overlap, the best the network can do is pick the vowel whose dots are most common there.
children: People tried for about seventy years to remove the differences between speakers, which is called **normalization**, without success. Hearing a lot of speech from the same speaker does help, because it gives the system more information about that person.

This overlap was first discovered in the early 1950s by **Peterson and Barney**. During the Second World War, spectrograms were kept secret by the military, and the overlap was found once spectrograms became available.

Good speech recognition only arrived around 2011 or 2012, using neural networks trained by backpropagation. Surprisingly, speech that changes over time turned out to be easier for modern systems than this frozen, one-moment problem.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Stochastic gradient descent** is the same method used to improve an average from data. Here it is used to improve every weight. It has the same **learning rate**, with the same tradeoff between learning fast and learning accurately.

**Dynamic programming** decides the order. The weights at the end are improved first, then the weights before them, and so on back to the beginning. So the easiest problem is solved first, and the hardest problem is solved last.
children: The error tells the network which way each output should move. Done, at about 56 percent, should go down. Dean should go up, and the other words should go down.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: For the last weights, one inner product connects each weight to the decision, so the direction of the change is clear. The network said done when the answer was dean. So any last weight that pushes done up should be **lowered**, and any last weight that pushes dean up should be **raised**.
children: A good exam answer says which way the weight should move and then explains why. Name the activation the weight multiplies and the output it feeds into.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **Backpropagation changes the last weights first, then the weights before them, and so on back to the first weights.** Each problem gets easier because something has already been learned from the problems solved before it.
children: Modern systems use this same method on about **six trillion weights**. That is what the huge data centers are doing.
**Geoffrey Hinton** won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Physics** for backpropagation. This idea is at the center of much of today's economy, and it has roots in physics through dynamical systems.
In plain terms, it is easiest to blame the weights closest to the mistake. That blame is then passed backward to the weights that came before them.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: Training uses **two matrices** of numbers. The first has one row per recording with **F1 and F2**. The second has a matching row of **zeros and a single one**, which marks the vowel the recording really was. During learning, the network picks a row, makes its decision, and compares it with the true answer. If the decision is wrong, the weights change.

**If the network makes the right decision, there is no error, so it has nothing to learn.** This can be a real problem. A network can keep getting the right answer by **memorizing** its data without learning the real pattern underneath. Stopping the learning at that point would be stopping too early.
Children learning English show the same thing, as **Carol Chomsky** observed in the early 1960s.
children: At first, very young children say **go** and **went** correctly, because they are just **memorizing** what they hear.
Then they notice the real pattern, that most English verbs make the past tense by adding a sound at the end, as in **jump** and **jumped**. So they start saying **goed**.
Later, they learn that some verbs are **exceptions**, and they get both the regular verbs and the exceptions right.
In plain terms, a right answer early on can come from memory, and real learning can show up as new mistakes.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: **The import lines bring into Python the programs for inner products, backpropagation and related work**, so none of that has to be written by hand. The exam can ask what these lines mean, but it will never ask you to write the program from scratch.
children: This works because of **libraries**. A library is a collection of programs written by one group that other people can use without knowing how they work inside. The idea of building software this way goes back to **Margaret Hamilton's** work on the software that flew **Apollo 11** to the moon.

Around 2015, **Facebook** released **PyTorch** and **Google** released **TensorFlow**. After that, researchers no longer had to write their own backpropagation code. Most people now use PyTorch, which is often just called torch.
The **load** lines read the formant matrix and the matching vowel matrix from files on the computer.

teaching.text: **Sequential means the network is a sequence of layers**, one after another. Every network covered so far is like this. A large language model is an example of a network that is not just a sequence of layers.
children: Each **Linear** line is one **processing layer**. A processing layer has weights and does inner products with the numbers coming in. The input layer does no processing, so the five layers need only **four lines**.
**nn.Linear(2, 3)** means "this layer receives information from 2 neurons, and it has 3 neurons." The other lines read the same way.
